items.title: LPG and the Changing Role of the State
items.body:
### LPG and the role of the state

**In one line**
LPG means the 1991 reforms — Liberalisation, Privatisation and Globalisation — that changed the Indian state from a controller that ran the economy into a regulator and facilitator that enables it.

**The story**
By 1991 India faced a severe balance-of-payments crisis — foreign reserves were almost empty. The **P. V. Narasimha Rao** government, with **Manmohan Singh** as Finance Minister, chose to open up the economy. The **New Industrial Policy, 1991** scrapped most industrial licences, ending the **Licence-Permit-Quota Raj** under which a business needed government permission for almost everything. The state stopped trying to produce and control, and instead focused on setting rules and delivering services — summed up in the slogan **'Minimum Government, Maximum Governance'**.

**Why it matters / why it is asked**
This is the governance core of the whole topic: who launched the reforms, what LPG stands for, and how the state's role changed are all common Prelims and Mains points.

**Picture it — the three strands of LPG**

| Strand | What it did |
|---|---|
| Liberalisation | Freed industry from licensing controls |
| Privatisation | Reduced the public sector through disinvestment |
| Globalisation | Integrated India with world trade and investment |

**Terms explained**
- **Licence-Permit-Quota Raj** — the pre-1991 system where businesses needed government licences, permits and quotas to operate or expand.
- **Disinvestment** — the government selling part of its ownership (equity) in a public-sector company.
- **'Steering not rowing'** — the idea that the state should guide (steer) the economy through rules, not run (row) it directly.

**Don't confuse**
- Rajiv Gandhi's government began limited liberalisation in the 1980s, but the full LPG reforms were launched in 1991 under Rao and Manmohan Singh.
- 'Minimum government' means less direct control, NOT abolishing the state or its welfare role.

**Remember it**
LPG opened three doors in 1991 — Licence-free, Private, Global — under Rao and Manmohan Singh.

**TL;DR**
- LPG = Liberalisation, Privatisation, Globalisation (1991 reforms).
- Launched under PM Narasimha Rao and FM Manmohan Singh after a balance-of-payments crisis.
- The New Industrial Policy 1991 dismantled the Licence-Permit-Quota Raj.
- The state shifted from producer/controller to regulator/facilitator.
- Captured in 'Minimum Government, Maximum Governance' and Ease of Doing Business.
keyPoints: LPG = Liberalisation (delicensing), Privatisation (disinvestment), Globalisation (world integration).
New Industrial Policy 1991 dismantled the Licence-Permit-Quota Raj.
Reforms launched in 1991 under PM Narasimha Rao and FM Manmohan Singh.
State role shifted from producer/controller to regulator/facilitator ('steering not rowing').
'Minimum Government, Maximum Governance' and Ease of Doing Business express this shift.
items.mnemonic: LPG = the three doors the 1991 reforms opened: Licence-free (L), Private (P), Global (G).

items.title: The Rise of the Regulatory State
items.body:
### The regulatory state

**In one line**
As the government stopped owning businesses, it set up independent referees — statutory regulators like SEBI and TRAI — to make the rules of each market and enforce them fairly.

**The story**
When the state ran industries itself, it was both player and umpire. After liberalisation, private firms entered sectors like stock markets, telecom and insurance, so a neutral umpire was needed. Parliament created **independent statutory regulators** that stand at arm's length from both the government and the companies they oversee — the hallmark of the **'regulatory state'**. At the same time the old monopoly-control law (MRTP) was replaced by a modern competition law, shifting the aim from curbing big firms to promoting fair competition.

**Why it matters / why it is asked**
Match-the-following questions on regulator-and-sector, and the shift from MRTP to the Competition Act, are frequently asked.

**Picture it — the main regulators**

| Regulator | Sector | Enabling law |
|---|---|---|
| SEBI | Securities market | SEBI Act, 1992 |
| TRAI | Telecom | TRAI Act, 1997 |
| IRDAI | Insurance | IRDA Act, 1999 |
| CCI | Competition / anti-trust | Competition Act, 2002 |

**Terms explained**
- **Statutory regulator** — a body set up by an Act of Parliament to supervise a particular market independently.
- **At arm's length** — able to act without day-to-day control by the government or the firms it regulates.
- **MRTP Act** — the Monopolies and Restrictive Trade Practices Act, the old law curbing monopolies, replaced by the Competition Act 2002.
- **Maharatna / Navratna / Miniratna** — grades giving strong public-sector firms more financial and operational autonomy.

**Don't confuse**
- SEBI (securities) is not IRDAI (insurance) — a common match-the-following trap.
- Disinvestment (selling equity) is different from granting Navratna autonomy (no equity sale).

**Remember it**
Four regulators by year: SEBI 1992, TRAI 1997, IRDAI 1999, CCI 2002.

**TL;DR**
- Liberalisation created independent regulators to govern markets at arm's length.
- SEBI (1992) securities; TRAI (1997) telecom; IRDAI (1999) insurance; CCI (2002 Act) competition.
- Disinvestment (via DIPAM) dilutes government equity — minority vs strategic sale.
- Maharatna/Navratna status grants autonomy to strong PSUs.
- MRTP Act replaced by the Competition Act, 2002 — from curbing monopoly to promoting competition.
keyPoints: Liberalisation created independent regulators to govern markets at arm's length ('regulatory state').
SEBI (1992) — securities; TRAI (1997) — telecom; IRDAI (1999) — insurance; CCI (2002 Act) — competition.
Disinvestment (via DIPAM) dilutes government equity in PSUs — minority vs strategic sale.
Maharatna/Navratna status grants operational and financial autonomy to strong PSUs.
MRTP Act replaced by the Competition Act, 2002 — from curbing monopoly to promoting competition.

items.title: Impact on Federalism
items.body:
### Impact on federalism

**In one line**
Liberalisation made the states more powerful economic players — they now compete with each other for investment (competitive federalism) while also working jointly with the Centre in new forums (cooperative federalism).

**The story**
Before 1991 the Centre allocated industrial licences, so states had little say over where factories went. Once licensing ended, a state could attract a factory directly by offering land, incentives and quick clearances. States therefore began to **compete for investment and foreign capital** — competitive federalism. Later, new institutions were built so the Centre and states could decide big questions together, especially after the Goods and Services Tax required shared taxation.

**Why it matters / why it is asked**
The difference between competitive and cooperative federalism, and the bodies that embody each (NITI Aayog, GST Council, Inter-State Council), are standard exam points.

**Picture it — cooperative-federalism forums**

| Body | Basis | Function |
|---|---|---|
| NITI Aayog | Executive resolution, 2015 | Policy think-tank; replaced the Planning Commission |
| GST Council | Art 279A (101st Amendment, 2016) | Joint decisions on indirect taxes |
| Inter-State Council | Art 263 | Centre-state coordination |

**Terms explained**
- **Competitive federalism** — states competing with one another to attract investment through better policies and faster clearances.
- **Cooperative federalism** — the Centre and states working together on shared policy.
- **Business Reforms Action Plan** — the exercise that ranks states on ease of doing business, institutionalising competition.
- **GST Council** — the constitutional body (Article 279A) where the Centre and states jointly fix indirect-tax rates.

**Don't confuse**
- NITI Aayog is based on an executive resolution (2015); the GST Council is a constitutional body (Article 279A).
- Reforms made states more relevant, NOT less — a common wrong statement.

**Remember it**
Competitive = states versus states for capital; cooperative = Centre plus states deciding together.

**TL;DR**
- Liberalisation empowered states as economic actors competing for investment.
- Competitive federalism is institutionalised via Ease of Doing Business / Business Reforms Action Plan rankings.
- NITI Aayog (2015) replaced the Planning Commission and promotes cooperative and competitive federalism.
- The GST Council (Art 279A) is a joint Centre-state fiscal body.
- States became more relevant, not less, under reforms.
keyPoints: Liberalisation empowered states as economic actors competing for investment ('competitive federalism').
Institutionalised via Ease of Doing Business / Business Reforms Action Plan state rankings.
NITI Aayog (2015) replaced the Planning Commission and promotes cooperative & competitive federalism.
GST Council (Art 279A) is a joint Centre-state fiscal decision-making body.
States became more relevant, not less, under reforms.

items.title: Welfare State, Civil Society & Accountability
items.body:
### Welfare, civil society and accountability

**In one line**
After liberalisation the state did not stop helping the poor — it changed how, moving from broad subsidies to targeted cash transfers, while NGOs, courts and the RTI Act grew to keep it accountable.

**The story**
Critics feared liberalisation would mean abandoning welfare. Instead the welfare state was **reconfigured**: rather than subsidising prices for everyone (which leaks to the non-poor), the government built a digital system to send money straight to the intended person's bank account. At the same time, as the state pulled back from direct provision and citizens grew more rights-conscious, **civil society, NGOs and Public Interest Litigation** expanded, and new transparency tools like the **RTI Act 2005** gave citizens the means to hold officials to account.

**Why it matters / why it is asked**
The JAM-DBT model, the rights-based laws of this era, and the growth of RTI/PIL/civil society are commonly tested.

**Picture it — the JAM trinity**

| Letter | Stands for | Role |
|---|---|---|
| J | Jan Dhan | A bank account for every household |
| A | Aadhaar | A unique identity number |
| M | Mobile | A phone to confirm and receive |

**Terms explained**
- **JAM trinity** — Jan Dhan accounts + Aadhaar identity + Mobile phones, the digital base for cash transfers.
- **DBT (Direct Benefit Transfer)** — paying a subsidy or benefit straight into the beneficiary's bank account.
- **PIL (Public Interest Litigation)** — a case filed in court by any citizen for the public good, not only for personal interest.
- **Social audit** — citizens checking official records against actual work (mandatory under MGNREGA).

**Don't confuse**
- Welfare was reconfigured (targeted), NOT abolished — rights-based laws like MGNREGA (2005) and RTE (2009) actually expanded in this era.
- DBT reduces leakage; it is not the same as cutting welfare spending.

**Remember it**
JAM = Jan Dhan + Aadhaar + Mobile, the three rails that carry DBT to the poor.

**TL;DR**
- Welfare was reconfigured, not abolished — from universal subsidy to targeted delivery.
- JAM trinity = Jan Dhan + Aadhaar + Mobile, powering Direct Benefit Transfer.
- Rights-based welfare expanded alongside markets (MGNREGA 2005, RTE 2009).
- The liberalisation era saw growth of NGOs, civil society and PIL.
- Accountability tools grew: RTI Act 2005, social audit, citizen charters (Sevottam).
keyPoints: Welfare was reconfigured, not abolished — from universal subsidy to targeted delivery.
JAM trinity = Jan Dhan + Aadhaar + Mobile, powering Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT).
Rights-based welfare expanded alongside markets (MGNREGA 2005, RTE 2009).
Liberalisation era saw growth of NGOs, civil society and PIL.
Accountability tools grew: RTI Act 2005, social audit, citizen charters (Sevottam).

items.title: Social Impact, Sovereignty & Critiques
items.body:
### Social impact, sovereignty and critiques

**In one line**
Liberalisation brought real gains like a bigger middle class, but also real costs like inequality and 'jobless growth', and it limited (without ending) India's freedom to set its own economic policy.

**The story**
The reforms unleashed fast growth — a booming services and IT sector, a rising middle class and more consumer choice. But growth did not create enough jobs, inequality widened, and much employment stayed in the unprotected informal sector. On the world stage, joining bodies like the **WTO** meant accepting rules that limit how freely India can frame some domestic policies — a debate about whether sovereignty is *conditioned* or truly *lost*. India keeps its constitutional authority and bargains hard, for example defending its food-subsidy and public-stockholding programmes.

**Why it matters / why it is asked**
'Jobless growth', inequality and the sovereignty debate are favourite critical-analysis points for both Prelims statements and Mains answers.

**Picture it — gains versus costs**

| Gains | Costs |
|---|---|
| Middle-class expansion | Rising inequality |
| Services and IT boom | 'Jobless growth' |
| Consumer choice | Large informal sector |
| Long-run poverty decline | Urban-rural and regional divides |

**Terms explained**
- **Jobless growth** — the economy's output (GDP) grows strongly, but employment does not grow in step.
- **Informal sector** — workers without written contracts, social security or job protection.
- **Policy space** — the room a government has to make its own economic policies.
- **Conditioned sovereignty** — sovereignty that still exists but is limited by treaty commitments.

**Don't confuse**
- Globalisation conditions sovereignty (limits policy space); it does NOT remove a state's constitutional authority.
- 'Jobless growth' means growth with too few jobs — not a fall in GDP, and not jobs without output.

**Remember it**
Reforms are debated on pace, sequencing and inclusiveness — not on whether to reverse their direction.

**TL;DR**
- Gains: middle-class expansion, consumer choice, services/IT growth, long-run poverty decline.
- Costs: rising inequality, jobless growth, large informal sector, urban-rural/regional divides.
- Globalisation conditions (does not eliminate) sovereignty — policy space shrinks under treaties.
- The state keeps constitutional authority and negotiates trade-offs (e.g. agri subsidies at the WTO).
- The core debate is now the pace, sequencing and inclusiveness of reform.
keyPoints: Gains: middle-class expansion, consumer choice, services/IT growth, long-run poverty decline.
Costs: rising inequality, jobless growth, large informal sector, urban-rural/regional divides.
Globalisation conditions (not eliminates) sovereignty — 'policy space' shrinks under treaty commitments.
State keeps constitutional authority and negotiates trade-offs (e.g. agri subsidies at WTO).
Core debate is now pace, sequencing and inclusiveness of reform, not its direction.

items.title: PYQ Precision — WTO, FEMA, FRBM & Industrial Policy
items.body:
### High-frequency exam facts

**In one line**
Four precise facts the exam repeats: India and the WTO, the FERA-to-FEMA switch, the FRBM fiscal law, and what the 1991 Industrial Policy did (and did not) do.

**The story**
As part of globalisation India joined the new **World Trade Organization** when it started in 1995, and replaced its harsh foreign-exchange law (FERA) with a milder one (FEMA) in 1999. To keep government borrowing in check it later passed the **FRBM Act 2003**. The 1991 Industrial Policy did the big delicensing, but the famous PSU 'Ratna' grades came years afterwards — a detail examiners love to test.

**Why it matters / why it is asked**
These are exact previous-year points where mixing up a year or an acronym flips the answer.

**Picture it — the four facts**

| Topic | Key fact |
|---|---|
| WTO | India a founder member; WTO began 1 January 1995 (from GATT) |
| FEMA | FERA 1973 replaced by FEMA 1999 (violations became civil) |
| FRBM | 2003 Act sets statutory deficit-reduction targets |
| Industrial Policy 1991 | Delicensing; reserved industries cut from 17 to 8 |

**Terms explained**
- **WTO** — the World Trade Organization, which sets and enforces global trade rules (began 1 January 1995).
- **FERA / FEMA** — the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act 1973 (strict, criminal) and the Foreign Exchange Management Act 1999 (liberal, civil).
- **FRBM Act** — the Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management Act 2003, which limits government deficits by law.
- **Ratna grades** — Navratna (from 1997), Maharatna (from 2010) and Miniratna autonomy tiers for public-sector firms.

**Don't confuse**
- The PSU Ratna grades (Navratna 1997, Maharatna 2010) came AFTER 1991 — they were not part of the New Industrial Policy 1991.
- FEMA treats forex breaches as civil matters; FERA had treated them as criminal.

**Remember it**
'1995 WTO, 1999 FEMA, 2003 FRBM' — the three dates of globalisation-era law.

**TL;DR**
- India was a founder member of the WTO (began 1 January 1995 from GATT).
- FERA 1973 was replaced by FEMA 1999 (forex violations became civil, not criminal).
- FRBM Act 2003 sets statutory fiscal-discipline targets.
- New Industrial Policy 1991 abolished licensing and cut reserved industries from 17 to 8.
- PSU Ratna grades came after 1991; disinvestment is run by DIPAM.
keyPoints: India was a founder member of the WTO (began 1 Jan 1995 from GATT).
FERA 1973 was replaced by FEMA 1999 (forex violations became civil, not criminal).
FRBM Act 2003 sets statutory fiscal-discipline/deficit-reduction targets.
New Industrial Policy 1991 abolished licensing and cut reserved industries from 17 to 8.
PSU Ratna grades (Navratna 1997, Maharatna 2010) came after 1991; disinvestment is run by DIPAM.
items.source: UPSC 2011/2019 Prelims; WTO; FERA/FEMA; FRBM Act 2003; New Industrial Policy 1991

items.title: Wealth Concentration (DPSP) & Gandhism–Marxism
items.body:
### Wealth concentration and the ideology debate

**In one line**
The Constitution's Directive Principles ask the state to stop wealth piling up in a few hands, and both Gandhism and Marxism ultimately want a society that needs no coercive state.

**The story**
The makers of the Constitution worried that free markets could let a few people corner most of the wealth. So the **Directive Principles** (Article 39) tell the state to spread resources for the common good — a built-in counterweight to the inequality that LPG-era markets can create. On the question of the state itself, two very different ideologies reach a similar end point: Gandhi wanted self-governing villages where power is held in trust, and Marx predicted the state would 'wither away' once classes disappeared.

**Why it matters / why it is asked**
The exact article (39(b) and (c)) and the Gandhism-Marxism convergence are repeat objective-type points.

**Picture it — the two ideas**

| Idea | Key point |
|---|---|
| Article 39(b) | Resources should serve the common good |
| Article 39(c) | The economy should not concentrate wealth to the common detriment |
| Gandhism | Stateless ideal via self-regulating villages and trusteeship |
| Marxism | Stateless ideal via the withering away of the state |

**Terms explained**
- **DPSP (Directive Principles of State Policy)** — guidelines the state should follow; courts cannot enforce them.
- **Trusteeship** — Gandhi's idea that the wealthy should hold their wealth in trust for society.
- **Withering away of the state** — Marx's idea that the state becomes unnecessary and dissolves in a classless society.

**Don't confuse**
- Article 39(b) and (c) are Directive Principles (non-justiciable), not Fundamental Rights.
- Gandhism and Marxism share the stateless goal but reach it by opposite means — moral/decentralist versus material/class-based.

**Remember it**
'39(b) common good, 39(c) no concentration'; Gandhi and Marx both end at a stateless society.

**TL;DR**
- Article 39(b) and (c) direct that resources serve the common good and wealth not be concentrated to the common detriment.
- These Directive Principles are a counterweight to LPG-era inequality.
- Gandhism and Marxism both envisage an eventual stateless society.
- Gandhi's route is moral and decentralist; Marx's is material and class-based.
keyPoints: Article 39(b) & (c) direct that resources serve the common good and wealth not be concentrated to the common detriment.
These Directive Principles are a counterweight to LPG-era inequality.
Gandhism and Marxism both envisage an eventual stateless society.
Gandhi's route is moral/decentralist (trusteeship); Marx's is material/class-based (withering away of the state).
items.source: UPSC/APPSC PYQ residual (review-v2 R2); Constitution Art 39

items.title: For Mains — Impact of LPG on Governance
items.body:
## For Mains — the analytical frame

Mains (Paper-III, Indian polity & governance — LPG impact on governance; statutory, regulatory and quasi-judicial bodies) rewards analysis of **how the state's role changed**, assessed across federalism, regulation, welfare and sovereignty — not a narration of 1991 economics.

| Dimension | What to write |
|---|---|
| Nature of change | Controller/producer → regulator/facilitator ('steering not rowing'); 'Minimum Government, Maximum Governance' |
| Regulatory state | Arm's-length regulators (SEBI 1992, TRAI 1997, IRDAI 1999, CCI 2002); MRTP → Competition Act |
| Federalism | Competitive federalism (states court FDI, BRAP rankings) + cooperative federalism (NITI Aayog 2015, GST Council Art 279A) |
| Welfare | Reconfigured, not abolished — JAM/DBT targeting; rights-based MGNREGA 2005, RTE 2009 |
| Criticism / limits | Jobless growth, inequality, informal-sector precarity, agrarian distress; regulatory accountability deficits; conditioned sovereignty (WTO) |
| Way forward | Accountable, well-staffed regulators; inclusive growth; strengthen fiscal federalism; social protection with social audit |

**Data points / reports / institutions to quote**
- New Industrial Policy 1991 (reserved industries 17 → 8); FRBM Act 2003.
- Regulators: SEBI (1992), TRAI (1997), IRDAI (1999), CCI (Competition Act 2002).
- WTO (founder, 1995); FERA 1973 → FEMA 1999.
- NITI Aayog (2015), GST Council (Art 279A); JAM/DBT; MGNREGA 2005.
- DPSP Article 39(b)(c) as the equity counterweight.

**AP angle**
Andhra Pradesh is a vivid facilitator-state case: aggressive investment promotion, industrial corridors and single-window clearances to court capital, set against large welfare-pension and SHG-based social protection — the twin pull of 'facilitate growth' and 'protect the vulnerable'.

**Use in answers**
- Thesis: 1991 was a change in the state's *role*, not a retreat from responsibility.
- Map each dimension (regulation, federalism, welfare) to a concrete institution.
- Quote 'steering not rowing' and Article 39(c) for balance.
- Diagram idea: a before/after arrow — 'Controller state (licence raj)' → 'Regulatory/facilitator state (regulators + DBT)'.
- Close with inclusive-growth and regulatory-accountability as the way forward.
keyPoints: Thesis: 1991 changed the state's role (controller → regulator/facilitator), not its responsibility.
Cover four dimensions: regulatory state, federalism, reconfigured welfare, conditioned sovereignty.
Quote regulators (SEBI/TRAI/IRDAI/CCI), NITI Aayog/GST Council, JAM/DBT, FRBM 2003.
Criticism: jobless growth, inequality, informal precarity, regulatory accountability gaps.
AP case study: investment promotion and corridors versus welfare pensions and SHGs.
Close with inclusive growth and accountable regulation as the way forward.
items.source: NCERT Indian Economic Development; 2nd ARC; NITI Aayog; regulator statutes; Constitution Art 279A & 39
